note: How `skynet setup --robot <model>` turns a model name into a driver library, and how far each driver has been tested. Two fields say what an installed robot needs (DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md F185, 12.B): transport is how the driver reaches its robot — ip (TCP, UDP, DDS, HTTP), can (SocketCAN) or raw (raw Ethernet frames, EtherCAT), or empty when it needs no network device (a serial bus, a simulated body in the same process) — because skynetk.service runs in a private network namespace that install.sh opens for exactly those and no more; python, on a driver of kind python, is the module drivers/python-host serves, the package directories (relative to drivers/) that install.sh puts on the robot, and the Python distributions the robot must already have. Kinds: prebuilt (builds with make alone; the wizard uses it built, or says how to build it), sdk (links a vendor SDK named in sdk; used built, or refused with the variable), cargo (a Rust driver in the workspace; found in the checkout's target/release, or refused with the cargo command for crate), sim (simulation-only; refused with the reason), python (runs under drivers/python-host; refused with the pointer), host (python-host itself: not a robot), library (shared code other drivers link: not a robot; linked_by names the models that are, and the refusal points at them), unmapped (no install mapping yet; refused with the README). Shipped in release bundles so the refusals work without a checkout. lib is always the Linux name: a library built on Windows or macOS will not run on the robot. Release stages (DRY-COVERAGE-PLAN.md Decisions 19): every driver that commands a physical robot carries a stage — alpha (never run on a physical robot; dry-tested only against counterparts written in this repository), beta (never run on a physical robot; dry-tested against software this repository did not write that speaks the robot's own interface — the maker's controller software, the maker's simulator, or an independent implementation of the protocol — which substrate names as the command the nightly substrate workflow runs) or stable (has run on a physical robot; no driver has, and tools/check-release-stages.mjs refuses the word until one does). tested_against says what the stage rests on. A driver that hosts other vendors' code per body (ros2_control) carries bodies instead, each with its own stage. hardware false marks a body that drives no hardware by design (mock, pendant), which carries no stage.

mavlink.note: an ArduPilot multirotor, fixed wing, ground rover, surface boat or submarine, or a PX4 multirotor, fixed wing or ground rover, over MAVLink, command-level; runs under drivers/python-host
mavlink.tested_against: ArduPilot's own flight code built for x86 (SITL, 4.7.1 at a pinned commit): a multirotor, a rover, a surface boat, a submarine (ArduSub, moved by sticks, with a stop its configuration names) and a fixed wing armed, moved and stopped through the real ABI, with the reference MAVLink implementation reading the same vehicle on a second serial port and the link impaired with delay, jitter and loss; and PX4's own published SIH image (a pinned digest): a multirotor, a fixed wing and a rover armed, moved and stopped through the real ABI, with the reference reading the same vehicle on PX4's second MAVLink instance. Both are the firmware on a simulated board and not a flight controller: no motors, no sensor noise, no radio, and a boat's stop is HOLD, which stops the thrust and not the hull. The submarine's depth is that simulator's weakest part (its pressure sensor reads negative absolute pressure and its depth swings by metres in seconds with nothing commanded), so its vertical axis is checked by what the firmware reads off the stick and not by where the vehicle goes

ros2_base.note: a ROS 2 mobile base over its velocity-command and odometry topics, command-level; runs under drivers/python-host and needs a sourced ROS 2 install (rclpy) wherever it runs
ros2_base.tested_against: ros2_control's own diff_drive_controller on its own mock hardware, in ROS 2 Jazzy (which takes a TwistStamped) and Humble (which takes a plain Twist), with a second reader of the same base written without this repository's code and ROS's own command-line tools reading the graph, and the sim half of SCTS through the real ABI; and ROBOTIS's own TurtleBot3 simulation (Gazebo, the burger's differential-drive plugin, its bridge) and iRobot's own Create 3 simulation (Gazebo, the maker's `motion_control` safety node and controller) with Gazebo's own pose of the model as the second opinion, which are the makers' simulations of robots and not the robots. The controller is the standard implementation of the two topics every wheeled-base stack speaks, and not any base maker's software: Husky, TurtleBot 4, Stretch and the rest are claimed from their documentation and not run, and the hardware is mock_components/GenericSystem, which is never late, never stalled and has no inertia or slip

ros_industrial.note: a robot arm behind a ROS-Industrial simple_message server (the protocol of Motoman's MotoROS, abb_driver's RAPID server, fanuc_driver and others); runs under drivers/python-host
ros_industrial.tested_against: ROS-Industrial's own simple_message library (industrial_core, built from source at a pinned commit, without ROS) as a controller's server, in each of the four ways a controller's build can spell an int and a real (little- or big-endian, 4- or 8-byte reals): the library's sockets, framing, codecs, message manager, ping handler and reconnect are the maker's, and the arm behind them is a straight-line interpolator written here. The driver's bytes are held to the library's, built and run, in both directions (118 checks), and the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI against each build. It is an independent implementation of the protocol written by the people who wrote it and not any robot maker's controller: Yaskawa Motoman, ABB, Fanuc, Staubli and the rest are claimed from ROS-Industrial's and each maker's documentation and not run, the protocol carries no joint limits or model so the arm's own go in the configuration, and what a controller does with a trajectory point is its vendor's

reachy_mini.note: a Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini (the head's six degrees of freedom, the body's yaw and the two antennas: nine scalar joints) over its daemon's own REST interface; runs under drivers/python-host
reachy_mini.tested_against: Pollen Robotics' own daemon in its own simulator (`reachy-mini-daemon --sim`, the maker's package at a pinned commit installed with its MuJoCo extra and its Git LFS meshes, run headless in a container): the physics, the kinematics, the REST interface and the web server are the maker's. The driver's routes, models and limits are held to the maker's source and run through the maker's own pydantic models (30 checks); the driver's session, commands, refusals and stop run against that daemon with the maker's models, its physics and its web server's access log as the second opinion (39 checks); the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI against it (34 of 34). Not run: a robot, Wireless or Lite. The maker's simulator does not model motor torque (its `get_motor_control_mode` returns a constant), so `limp` is held to the request its server received and not to a head that went limp; the motors' firmware, heat, cables and the real antenna travel are not reached; the ranges of the head's translation and of the antennas are the operator's, because the maker documents none

schunk.note: a SCHUNK EGU, EGK or EZU gripper (one prismatic jaw) over its module's own web interface, the EtherNet/IP and EtherCAT modules; a PROFINET module is refused by name; runs under drivers/python-host
schunk.tested_against: SCHUNK's own protocol simulator (`schunk_gripper_dummy`) and its own client (`schunk_gripper_library`), both installed from the maker's repository at a pinned commit and run in a container: an EGU 60 and an EGK 25 on EtherNet/IP and an EGU 60 on PROFINET. The driver's bytes are held to the maker's client, which is run (21 checks); the driver's session, handshake, refusals, grips, both stops and an outage run against the maker's simulator with the maker's client as the second opinion and a record of every frame its server was handed (83 checks); the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI against it (37 passed, 0 failed). Not run: a gripper, an EZU, an EtherCAT or PROFINET module, or the maker's firmware. The maker's simulator is minimal and four things about it were measured: it comes up in a fast stop, drops ready-for-operation on every write, does not stop a motion it is told to stop, and does not replace a motion in flight (the newer command can be lost); so a stop is held to the frame the module was handed and the error it reports, never to the jaw halting, and grip force in newtons, a workpiece, and the jaw's dynamics are not reached

robotiq.note: a Robotiq 2F-85 or Hand-E adaptive gripper (one prismatic jaw) over Modbus RTU, on its own RS-485 line (a USB adapter); a gateway that forwards the line raw over TCP is reached by installing with install.sh --driver-transport ip by hand, and a 2F-140, or either gripper with other fingers, is `model: custom` with a profile the operator measured; runs under drivers/python-host
robotiq.tested_against: Robotiq's own C++ SDK (github.com/Robotiq/grippers at a pinned commit, built unmodified in a container) and its own simulated gripper, a register model behind its own Modbus RTU server, served on a TCP port and a pseudo-terminal, with the maker's own client reading the same gripper. The driver's bytes are held to the maker's client, which is run (43 checks: 500 random commands in each of three functions, 1,512 status blocks, the replies, the conversions and the fault tables, and the maker's whole client driving the simulated gripper written here); the driver's activation, commands, both motions, the stop, a gateway that goes away and a gripper that comes back with no activation, and twenty fault bytes staged in the maker's own register model run against the maker's simulated gripper with the maker's client as the second opinion and a record of every request its server was handed (56 checks); the sim half of SCTS passes through the real ABI against it (37 passed, 0 failed). Not run: a gripper, a 2F-140, an RS-485 adapter or the maker's firmware. The maker's simulated gripper models no motion, no object and no fault of its own (activation completes instantly and the fingers are wherever they were told), so motion, a workpiece, a status that lags its command and a fault the gripper raises itself are held to a simulated gripper written in this repository; and the grip force is a fraction of a range the driver cannot see, never in newtons

odrive.note: ODrive servo axes (a v3 board carries two) over the CANSimple protocol on one CAN bus, joint-level; runs under drivers/python-host
odrive.tested_against: simulated ODrive axes written in this repository, first on an in-process bus and then on a kernel virtual CAN bus against axes in another process: the wire, the enable walk, motion in position, velocity and torque with mixed per-joint modes, the stop (which latches ESTOP_REQUESTED in the firmware, so there is no software release and a new session returns the body) and the refusal of an axis with a latched fault, no heartbeat, or nothing on its node. The frame ids, payload layouts and enumerations are held to ODrive's own firmware, CAN database and enums module at a pinned commit by a layout check (96 checks), which also pins two disagreements between the maker's own sources (F280). Not run: an ODrive, any motor on an axis, or the maker's firmware
